seoTitle: How to Create a Udemy Course From Start to Finish
metaDescription: Ready to teach on Udemy? Learn how to validate your course idea, walk through the course-creation wizard, produce content, and market it once it's live.
intro:
Creating a Udemy course starts before you touch a camera, with the instructor dashboard and a short setup wizard that shapes how Udemy positions the course from day one. The early screens ask for a working title and a weekly time commitment, and answering them honestly makes the production work that follows easier.

This guide walks through those wizard screens, then covers producing, structuring, and marketing the finished course. It's written for anyone new to course creation, whether the goal is teaching a niche skill or building a second income stream.

steps.heading: Brainstorm and validate your course idea
steps.body: Before opening Udemy, pick a topic that can be taught with real depth and check that demand exists for it. Search existing Udemy courses in the same space to see how many students they've drawn and what reviews say is missing. A crowded category is not automatically a bad sign: it usually means a proven audience already exists, and the job becomes finding an angle those existing courses cover poorly.

steps.heading: Open your instructor dashboard
steps.body: Once signed in as an instructor, the Courses tab lists everything published or started, each with its status marked clearly. A course still in progress shows as DRAFT next to a progress bar reading "Finish your course." The New course button sits top-right on this same page, and clicking it starts the creation flow. An abandoned draft also lives here, so there's no need to start over if one was left half-finished.

image.caption: The instructor Courses dashboard, listing an existing draft course and a New course button to start another.

steps.heading: Work through the course-creation wizard
steps.body: Clicking New course opens a short, numbered wizard with a progress bar at the top. Step 2 asks for a working title, and Udemy says directly that it doesn't need to be final: the placeholder text notes it can be changed later, so there's no reason to stall here writing a perfect headline. Type something descriptive enough to stay oriented and move on. The title can be refined once the finished course shows what it really covers.

image.caption: Step 2 of the course-creation wizard, asking for a working title with a note that it can be changed later.

steps.heading: Answer Udemy's planning questions honestly
steps.body: The wizard's last step asks how much time can realistically go into building the course each week, with options from "I'm very busy right now (0-2 hours)" up to "I have lots of flexibility (5+ hours)." This is not a productivity test. Udemy uses the answer to calibrate the guidance and milestones shown afterward, so an accurate answer produces a more realistic production timeline than one built assuming more free time than is really available.

image.caption: The last step of the wizard, asking how many hours per week you can dedicate to building the course.

steps.heading: Create your video content
steps.body: With the course shell created, move to recording. Lessons that walk through one concept at a time tend to outperform long, unstructured recordings: production quality and pacing directly affect how students perceive and stick with a course. Keep individual videos focused. A five-minute lesson covering exactly one idea beats a twenty-minute one that wanders across three.

steps.heading: Structure your course material
steps.body: Organize recorded lessons into sections that build on each other logically instead of dropping every video into one long list. Udemy's course builder groups lessons into sections and lectures, and students engage far better with a course that has clear checkpoints than one that feels like a single unbroken stream of content.

steps.heading: Market your course after it's live
steps.body: Publishing is not the finish line. Visibility matters as much as content quality once a course goes live. Promote it through Udemy's own marketing tools, share it in communities where the target audience already spends time, and keep refining it based on the questions and reviews students leave.

faq.question: Do I need prior teaching experience to create a Udemy course?
faq.answer: No. The course-creation wizard is aimed at beginners and doesn't assume prior teaching experience to get started.

faq.question: How do I know if my course topic has enough demand?
faq.answer: Search Udemy for existing courses on the same topic. A high student count shows demand, and the reviews on those courses usually point straight at what they leave out, which is the gap a new course can fill.

faq.question: How long does it take to create a Udemy course?
faq.answer: Timelines vary by course length and complexity. Udemy asks upfront how many hours per week can realistically go into the course, and uses that answer to set more realistic pacing expectations.

faq.question: How do I make money from a Udemy course?
faq.answer: Publishing a course lets an instructor monetize their expertise directly, on top of building visibility and credibility in their subject.

verifiedNote: Screens and click path come from a recorded walkthrough of the instructor Courses dashboard and the New Course wizard. This revision trims the previous version's unverified aside about AI-assisted editing tools, tightens the prose, and reduces overlap with the companion guide on uploading a finished course.
